messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Laura is a 48-year-old single woman who works in social ministry, much of her week spent moving between church offices, food pantry spaces, hospital rooms, and community meetings where she helps people in crisis find practical support. The event she returns to in session is a life-threatening car accident that happened while she was being transported by someone else. What remains most vivid to her is not only the violence of the impact but the fact that she had no control over what was happening. She describes the sickening moment of realizing the car was committed to the collision and that she could not stop it, get out, or make her body do anything useful. When she speaks about it, the image that comes back most sharply is of cars smashed together at impossible angles, the kind of scene she still cannot pass on the road without feeling herself go rigid.

In the weeks afterward, Laura found that reminders were not abstract. Seeing wrecked cars, even in ordinary traffic after a minor fender-bender, could pull her immediately into the sense that catastrophe was right there again. Feeling physically unwell was another powerful cue. If she became dizzy, nauseated, weak, or even vaguely “off,” her mind went straight to danger. She had come to feel that her body could not be counted on anymore, that physical sensations were warnings she had to obey. Situations that put her body under stress began to feel especially risky, so she started pulling back from exertion and anything that left her heart pounding or her muscles strained. Rest did not bring relief either. Relaxing felt dangerous to her, as if letting her guard down would leave her exposed to whatever might happen next. She stayed busy, alert, and braced.

Her work repeatedly places her in exactly the kinds of settings where these reactions show themselves. Entering a hospital room, a parish hall, or a crowded service office, Laura automatically looks for exits first. She notices doorways, stairwells, and the clearest route out before she can focus on the conversation she is there to have. In meetings, she prefers seats near the door and feels unsettled if someone else chooses for her or if she is expected to remain somewhere without an easy way to leave. Being forced into anything now carries a particular charge. Even routine pressures from work—being told to ride along to an outreach site, being assigned somewhere without much notice, being urged to “just sit and take a breath”—can stir an immediate inner resistance that feels larger than the moment. Other people’s reassurance does little. She says that when someone tells her she is safe, the words do not land; she cannot make herself believe them.

Over months, Laura’s world narrowed around transportation. She stopped driving whenever she could and avoided being a passenger as well. This created practical problems in a job that often depends on movement from place to place. She began rearranging her schedule, declining visits, and relying on others to cover parts of her work that once would have been routine for her. The consequences have been concrete and embarrassing to her. She worries that colleagues see her as difficult or unreliable, though she rarely explains more than that travel is “hard right now.” Ordinary sounds also catch her off guard. A dropped object in a church kitchen, a slammed car door outside the ministry office, a sudden noise in a hospital corridor can make her jump sharply, leaving her flushed and ashamed in front of others.

Alongside this, Laura carries a fixed sense of wrongness about what happened. She returns often to the unfairness of it—that her life was upended in an instant and, in her view, nothing meaningful has been done about it. She speaks about the accident with the conviction that bad things can happen without warning and that she has no real way to stop them. What frightens her most is not only another accident, but the idea that she could once again find herself trapped, dependent, and physically vulnerable, with her own body proving unreliable at the very moment she needs it.

She sought help after recognizing how much of her life had become organized around preventing exposure to the feelings she dreads. The immediate prompt was increasing difficulty carrying out her ministry work, especially when travel or unfamiliar buildings were involved. She is tired of planning every day around exits, transport, and whether her body feels steady enough. At the same time, she is afraid that treatment will ask her to surrender the vigilance that feels necessary to survive. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to forget the accident, but to move through her days without feeling that danger is waiting in every room, every bodily sensation, and every car on the road.
